page: Google Cloud Platform m3-megamem-64 is a memory-optimized server instance configured with 64 vCPUs and 976 GB of RAM. Powered by an Intel Xeon processor with an x86_64 architecture, it features 32 physical cores, 2 threads per core, and a dedicated CPU allocation running at a base speed of 2.6 GHz. The processor includes a 54 MB L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512 and cryptography acceleration via AES and SHA_NI. This instance does not include local storage or GPU hardware.

Benchmark data indicates strong multi-core and memory-intensive capabilities. The instance achieves strong results in multi-threaded Bzip3 decompression, Geekbench multi-core tests, and Passmark database operations. However, single-core performance remains in the average tier, as shown by stress-ng and Geekbench single-core metrics. Memory bandwidth is measured at 3255.75 GB/sec for cached small blocks and drops to 150.66 GB/sec for uncached large blocks. The lack of bundled local storage requires reliance on network-attached storage, which may introduce latency tradeoffs for I/O-heavy operations.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the m3-megamem-64 provides a high density of memory relative to compute resources, making it a specialized choice for memory-bound workloads rather than general-purpose compute. It is highly suited for large in-memory databases, enterprise resource planning systems, heavy data caching layers, and memory-intensive data processing pipelines that do not require GPU acceleration.
description: Google Cloud Platform m3-megamem-64 is an x86_64 memory-optimized server featuring 64 dedicated vCPUs and 976 GB of RAM, powered by a 2.6 GHz Intel Xeon processor with 32 physical cores. It lacks local storage and GPU accelerators, relying entirely on external storage. Performance benchmarks show strong multi-core execution, software compilation, and database operations, alongside average single-core performance. With a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 15.25 GB per core, this instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-bound workloads. It is best suited for large in-memory databases, caching layers, and memory-intensive data processing.
